extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and media/representation researchers interested in racialized portrayals in entertainment
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess instances of brownface and related practices (e.g., brown voice, stereotypical costuming, casting) in film, television, theatre, and comedy, taking into account historical context, community reception, and efforts toward authentic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of makeup to darken skin (brownface)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brownface is a social phenomenon in which a white or light-skinned person attempts to portray themselves as a 'brown' person of color, with a color imitating a light to dark brown complexion; it is typically defined as a racist phenomenon, similar to blackface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: actors applying dark makeup to appear more 'brown' (Bollywood examples such as Bala, Super 30; historical U.S. examples). Critique centers on the act of darkening skin as inherently tied to racist impersonation and caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stereotypical or exaggerated accents ('brown voice')
rubrics_metrics.description: "Brown voice" is the use of stereotypical, often exaggerated, accents when portraying a character with a Latin American, Middle Eastern, Polynesian, Native American, or Indian background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in cartoons and live-action; cited criticisms include Apu from The Simpsons (thick Indian accent voiced by a white actor) and Speedy Gonzales' thick accent. Evaluate whether accent relies on caricature or reduces a group to a comic trope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting authenticity (white actors portraying brown roles / whitewashing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Casting white or lighter-skinned actors to play brown characters, or altering white actors' appearance to read as brown, rather than casting ethnically appropriate performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable examples: Hank Azaria voicing Apu; Natalie Wood as Maria in West Side Story; Johnny Depp as Tonto; Joel Edgerton darkened for Ramses II; historical Hollywood whitewashing (Prince of Persia controversy). Consider both voice casting and on-screen casting, and examine whether roles were available to actors from the represented community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on stereotypical occupations, behaviors, and traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayals that present brown people as lazy, criminal, untrustworthy, unable to assimilate, or relegated to specific jobs (e.g., convenience store clerk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: José Jiménez portrayed as struggling to learn English, lazy and untrustworthy; Apu's convenience-store job criticized as stereotype. Assess whether character traits reinforce harmful generalizations rather than depicting complex individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stereotypical costume and visual markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing visual shorthand (e.g., poncho, sombrero, turbans, other props) to signal ethnicity in a reductive or mocking way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speedy Gonzales is dressed in a poncho and sombrero; such markers can cement caricatures. Evaluate whether costuming is worn for authenticity/respect or as caricatured shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and historical drivers (immigration, nativism, minstrelry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding brownface in light of historical and economic factors such as immigration policy, nativism, Bracero program, and the legacy of minstrel shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page links brownface emergence to the Chinese Exclusion Act, Bracero Program, Civil Rights-era shifts, and minstrel shows that mocked minorities for a white middle-class audience. Use historical context to evaluate why and how certain portrayals emerged and persisted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minstrelsy-style mockery intended to reassure dominant audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertainment that mocks minority groups (race, class, foreignness) to reassure the white middle-class audience of their social standing and normalcy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minstrel shows targeted the white middle class and used brownface/blackface to mock minorities. Evaluate whether a work's comedic frame functions to denigrate groups for the benefit of dominant-group affirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altering appearance by actors of partial descent to appear 'more' ethnic
rubrics_metrics.description: Light-skinned actors of partial or related descent using makeup/darkening to appear more like a historical or cultural figure (e.g., Ben Kingsley darkening to play Gandhi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ben Kingsley wore darker makeup to appear more like Gandhi; such choices raise questions about whether the alteration is respectful/necessary or reinforces problematic practices. Consider alternatives (casting a closer visual match) and audience perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community reception and reinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: How target communities perceive and respond to a character or depiction (rejection, acceptance, reclamation, or reinterpretation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speedy Gonzales has been embraced by parts of the Hispanic community for breaking certain stereotypes despite problematic origins. Assess whether a portrayal is critiqued by, or accepted within, the community it represents, and how that affects evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversy and public backlash as indicators of offensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances where public criticism, controversy, or media attention signal problematic representation (e.g., Paula Deen photo, debates over Apu, criticism of casting choices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use documented controversies (Paula Deen's son in brownface, The Problem with Apu documentary, coverage of whitewashing) as evidence of harm or offensiveness, while also considering the substance of criticisms rather than treating backlash as the sole metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efforts toward ethnically accurate representation and inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive practices that discourage brownface: casting and hiring members of the represented community, creating stories by insiders, and portraying characters in complex, non-stereotypical ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: shows like Master of None featuring Indian American creators and casts, government/affirmative action efforts, and increased involvement of Latinx creators leading to more accurate portrayals. Evaluate productions by their use of authentic voices, writers, directors, and performers.
